The findings reveal differences in performance across the technologies, offering valuable insights for developers and manufacturers in selecting appropriate materials for flexible and stretchable electronic applications.

articleTitle: Advanced Ultrathin Spray Coating Process Technology for Heterogeneous Integration Applications
abstract: In this work the spray coating deposition of thin and ultrathin homogeneous layers of Divinylsiloxane-bis-benzocyclobutene (DVS-BCB or BCB) is presented. Film thicknesses from 200 nm down to 5 nm are achieved. The layer thickness is assessed using Variable Angle Spectroscopy Ellipsometry (VASE), which allows for nondestructive high precision thickness measurement. Multiple positions mapping provides information about thickness distribution across the substrate. This spray coating process study reveals that the layer deposition for thicker films (> 75 nm) is mainly driven by hardware parameters. For thinner layers, additional material solution adjustment (dilution) is necessary. For each studied layer thickness (200 nm, 35 nm and 5 nm), batches of 25 wafers are prepared aiming to study the wafer-to-wafer process stability necessary for successful industrial application. Finally, the thin and ultrathin BCB layers are used for different bonding technologies, i.e. die-to-wafer permanent adhesive bonding as well as micro transfer printing (μ Tp). Multiple electronic integrated circuits (EICs) and quantum dot lasers (QDLs) devices are heterogeneously integrated to Si/SiO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>/BCB wafers using the layers with thicknesses of 35 nm and 5 nm. For all devices a 100 % process yield is obtained.

articleTitle: Adaptive Artificial Neural Networks for Power Loss Prediction in SiC MOSFETs
abstract: Silicon carbide (SiC) MOSFETs have become increasingly central in the development of high-efficiency power applications as a result of their unique properties. However, accurate modeling of power losses is a crucial aspect to fully benefit from the potential of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$S$</tex>iC MOSFETs. Power loss estimation for devices with different chip sizes is a key research field that accelerates the pre-design of new products and evaluates their performance across various applications without the need for extensive physical testing. In parallel to the establishment of SiC power devices, machine learning (ML) techniques, as a branch of artificial intelligence (AI), offer promising advancements in optimizing the design and performance of modern electronics. This paper investigates the application of selected machine learning methods, specifically standard artificial neural networks (ANNs) and adaptive artificial neural networks (a-ANNs), to estimate conduction and switching losses in SiC MOSFETs. Experimental measurements at different electrical and thermal conditions are the input dataset to train and test the developed algorithms. The performance of traditional polynomial regression models is compared with ANNs and a-ANNs. The prediction results demonstrate that machine learning-based models outperform traditional methods, especially when only part of the dataset is provided in the training phase. The a-ANNs are the most accurate and flexible modeling approach and excellently perform when predicting the loss characteristics for thermal and electrical conditions never encountered in the training dataset. More in detail, a-ANNs predict the target variables with low percentage errors in the 5% range. These findings highlight the potential of machine learning in improving the estimation accuracy of power losses in <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$S$</tex>iC MOSFETs. Similar algorithms can benefit additional fields in the power semiconductor world.

articleTitle: Study of Cross-Contamination in Multi-Chamber PVD Systems Used for High-Throughput Seed Layer Deposition
abstract: The increasingly higher interconnect density in modern WLP applications exponentially increases the importance of the interconnects quality as the critical dimensions shrink. The metric defining the quality of the interconnects is the contact resistance, Rc. UBM and RDL metallization are key fabrication steps that provide the routing between the I/O pads of the chip and the bumps. In high-volume manufacturing, the adhesion and seed layers necessary to fabricate UBM and RDL are deposited in multi-chamber PVD systems. Two industry standards are available: the Indexer and the Cluster type. In previous research, we reported on the performance of the Indexer delivering 50% lower Rc and 40% higher throughput compared to the Cluster counterpart. The novel aspect of this research is the investigation of the cross-contamination occurring in these competing platforms. RGA measurement is performed to study the propagation of the residual outgassing through the PVD systems during continuous run. SiO2 wafers are used as reference due to their negligible outgassing and compared to PBO coated wafers mimicking the outgassing of typical products with organic passivation. Experimental data has shown that the main source of contamination in both platforms is the residual outgassing of the etched PBO wafer being transported from one chamber to the next. In contrast, the cross-talk between chambers is marginal. Moreover, the faster chamber-to-chamber transfer time in the Indexer mitigates the risk of recontamination of the cleaned I/O contacts.

articleTitle: Simulation Analysis on Thermal Performance of a Lidless Fan-Out Package
abstract: As an emerging and competitive candidate, the fan-out package can meet the small form factor, high density and high electrical performance requirements of the state-of-the-art applications in mobile, 5G and AI. The fan-out package also offers high packaging flexibility for integration. While the demands in high performance of chip drive the power consumption and heat dissipation dramatically increased, the thermal management of the fan-out package is becoming a critical issue. In this paper, the thermal performance characterization of the fan-out package is performed by the 3D finite element method. A lidless structure with an integrated heatsink directly attached to the fan-out package is proposed. EMC after wafer level molding of fan-out package process can support the heatsink and control warpage as the stiffener rings attached to the package. There is a certain thickness of overmolded EMC which is often used as electrical insulation between the chip and the heatsink in the fan-out package structure for high-density system integration. Nevertheless, the poor thermal conductivity of EMC will be a bottleneck for the thermal dissipation performance. The differences in thermal performance without an EMC cap and with various thicknesses of EMC cap of the lidless fan-out package are systematically simulated. The thermal resistance models are extracted. The thermal resistance without the EMC cap is 0.25°C/W, and the thermal resistance with the cap thicknesses of 50μm, 100μm and 150μm are 1.86°C/W, 3.40°C/W and 4.89°C/W, respectively. The thermal resistance is positively proportional to the thickness of the EMC cap. The fan-out package without the EMC cap is better able to dissipate heat, while the fan-out package with the certain thickness of EMC cap wrapped on the chip results in poorer dissipation performance. The thermal simulation model of the lidded fan-out package is used for performance in comparison with the lidless. The thermal resistance of the lidless is much less than the lidded. Compared with the lidded, the lidless has a better thermal performance due to the removal of the lid and thermal interface material and the absence of their thermal interface. The heat generated by the chip can be directly dissipated to the heatsink. Therefore, the lidless structure of the fan-out package is presented as a thermal dissipation solution at package level and system level. The thermal performance of the lidless fan-out package with various height/counts/size of heatsink, air velocity and chip power is characterized.

articleTitle: Superconducting Superlattices for Cryogenic Systems
abstract: This study presents the development of highly thermally resistive interconnects for cryogenic integrated systems. These interconnects are based on a superconducting superlattice technology to enhance the thermal resistance via phonon interface scattering while maintaining perfect electrical conduction at low temperatures. After the qualification of single TiN and Nb films with critical temperatures of 4.9 K and 8.7 K respectively, superlattices with 5-period TiN/Nb bilayers were fabricated to morphologically, electrically and thermally evaluate the potential of this technology. These characterizations demonstrate an effective critical temperature of 8.4 K and compelling thermal properties at sub-K temperatures with a thermal conductivity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$9.7 \cdot 10^{-7} \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m} \cdot \mathrm{K}$</tex> at 1 K. The implementation of the super-conducting superlattice into 20 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu\mathrm{m}$</tex>-diameter interconnects in a two- tier demonstrator is then discussed.

articleTitle: Using µ-RAMAN Spectroscopy to Inspect Sintered Interconnects
abstract: To enable high operation temperature, sintering is the technology of choice for connecting the semiconductor die to the substrate for power electronic converters. Due to the mismatch of the coefficient of thermal expansion of die and ceramic based boards thermo-mechanical stress is created after sintering. Therefore, the mechanical properties, i.e. young's modulus and creep parameters, of the interconnect materials are essential for the reliability of the converters. µ-RAMAN spectroscopy (µ-RS) is a powerful tool to access the strain in the surface of semiconductors. In the present paper, the RAMAN shift is used to measure the strain in silicon test chips after bonding them to copper test boards. In the paper three different interconnect materials are investigated: eutectic AuSn soldering, Ag and Cu sintering. The AuSn interconnect is used as a benchmark because mechanical properties of eutectic AuSn solder including creep properties are well known. The packaging induced in plane stresses <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Delta \sigma (\Delta \sigma = {\sigma_{max}} - {\sigma_{min}})$</tex> are measured for the interconnect materials: high stress is revealed for very dense almost void free Ag interconnects using silver paste (Δ <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sigma$</tex>=880MPa) which is closed to those observed for AuSn soldering (Δ <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sigma$</tex>=920MPa). Significant lower stress values are measured for copper flake-based interconnects (Δ <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sigma$</tex>=700MPa). It was observed that the stress distribution of well sintered interconnects is very similar to the distribution in eutectic AuSn solder. Deviations from the theoretical stress distribution identified by µ-RS indicate sinter process deviations. For instance, asymmetric stress distribution can be caused by inhomogeneous densification of the paste due to inhomogeneous paste printing or tilt in the bond tool. For AuSn soldering a Finite Element Model (FEA) was validated by the authors previously using µ-RS. To simulate the stress distribution for sintered interconnects parameter sets for creep models (Anand and Garafalo) were taken from literature. It must be noted that the published parameters vary extremely (several order of magnitudes) which is hardly plausible. Most parameter sets couldn't reproduce the experimental results measured by µ-RS at all. This might be attributed to the fact that sintered interconnect may have quite different properties. Using the Anand parameter (model 1) [1] the stress distribution and creep relaxation of the Ag interconnects could be modelled in Ansys mechanical work bench very well. The approach opens the door to use µ-RAMAN as a tool to access the mechanical properties of new sinter interconnects to develop reliable power electronic modules.

articleTitle: Development of an Adaptive Re-Distribution Patterning Process for Fan-Out Packages with Embedded High I/O Components
abstract: A solution to manufacture high-performance electronic systems with computing intensive functions in volume constrained products, is the utilization of miniaturized microsystems equipped with state-of-the-art embedded components densely integrated in build-up substrates via advanced patterning processes. Besides the requirements like a sufficient yield of the lithographic process itself in order not to lose the valuable high-density components, a major point of an RDL-last approach is to register each layer of the production panel to the corresponding device during RDL fabrication. One solution is, to measure the deviation of the target position towards the actual position, then digitally reroute the connections and finally feed forward the data into the process tools like a direct imaging system (DI). This paper publishes results from the EU funded project CHARM where AT&S has supplied embedded components 25 mm x 17 mm x 110 µm into panels to FHG IZM which are further connected to upper RDL build-up layers, resulting into fan-out panel level packages (FOPLP) with enlarged pitches compared to pitches on the components. All process steps toward FOPLP packaging will be elucidated and solutions to all encountered challenges will be shown and discussed. At the end, the computing modules stacked with advanced power modules have been the heart of the ADPU units in automotive electronics for autonomous mining vehicles demanded by CHARM end-users.

articleTitle: Use of 3D Printing Techniques in the Development of Electronic Systems, Support Stage in the Digital Transformation of the Laboratories
abstract: The application of 3D printing technologies in electronics manufacturing covers a very wide range of techniques and applications. A less explored but relevant area is the application of low-cost 3D printing technologies in electronics manufacturing, not only as an alternative to the classical production of electronic circuits using PCBs but also as a multi-functional option for special applications requiring increased mechanical resistance to shock and extreme environmental conditions. In addition, this approach, used in teaching practice, requires students to merge various concepts and notions, from the electrical but also the mechanical field. It will be seen from the paper that they must understand both electric layout problems and the generation of a three-dimensional representation of an electronic circuit, but also mechanical design, compliant structures design and strength of materials, 3D printing problems, tolerances, technology (electronics and mechanics), vibrations and shocks damping solutions (passive and/or active and semi-active), thermal transfer. By carrying out a student project to develop a complete electronic circuit application embedded in a 3D printed structure, an excellent teaching tool is created for the practice of undergraduate and master's students. The paper analyzes the feasibility of cheap 3D printing solutions in making electronic circuits and presents the experience in using this technique in teaching practice. At the same time, it includes conclusions regarding the recommended directions for the development of the application to maximize the knowledge and skills developed by students.

Author Keywords: didactic application in mechatronics and electronics training

articleTitle: Coupled Electrothermal Analysis with Reduced Order Models for Optimizing GaN HEMTs Performance in Traction Inverters
abstract: In electric vehicle power electronics (PE) systems, particularly for traction inverters, it is pivotal to effectively manage electrical, thermal, and mechanical stresses experienced by Gallium Nitride (GaN) High Electron Mobility Transistors (HEMTs), under different operational conditions. Analysis of these stresses through simulations, enables initial assessments and optimizations before construction of physical prototypes and experimental testing. However, conventional simulation techniques like Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) demand significant processing resources and time, being disadvantageous in PE system-level simulations. A Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) thermal reduced order model (ROM) of an inverter phase leg module based on embedded GaN HEMT dies is considered in this research, as derived from 3D CFD transient thermal simulations. The ROM is coupled with a PLECS/MATLAB simulation of a full Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motor (PMSM) traction drive, including temperature dependency of GaN HEMT's drain source on-resistance, thus allowing fast coupled electrothermal simulations and accurate estimation of GaN HEMT temperature changes in response to generated power losses during varying torque/speed operations. The mechanical response of the inverter phase leg module in response to a critical thermal loading scenario (i.e., rapid acceleration and deceleration) highlights potential permanent deformation of the topside copper metalization layers and microvia interconnects. The proposed workflow allows a fast coupled electrothermal and thermomechanical simulation framework for optimization and rapid identification of critical conditions of next generation PE systems.

articleTitle: Highly Efficient Modeling of Solder Balls and Their Visco-plastic Behavior Applying the Energy Conserving Sampling and Weighting Method
abstract: The increasing complexity of automotive and industrial electronic control units does not allow the use of regular finite element analyses for complete design optimization regarding thermo mechanical reliability. In particular, the high number of solder balls, which require a fine resolution due to the non-linear material behavior, greatly increases the calculation effort. Therefore, this paper presents a new approach to obtain reduced models of the solder balls using the Energy Conserving Sampling and Weighting method. The method allows the combination of the reduced models with the remaining regular finite element model. This significantly reduces the calculation effort while maintaining high accuracy.

Author Keywords: Energy Conserving Sampling and Weighting Method

articleTitle: Advanced Wafer Singulation Techniques for Miniaturized Metal-oxide (MOX) Micro-hotplates Based Gas Analyzer
abstract: A typical process flow for micro-hotplate sensors includes the fabrication of the sensor wafer followed by functionalization. Functionalization involves the local deposition of a sensing material, or several materials in the case of a multi-gas analyzer. Functionalization makes the analyzer sensitive to specific gases. Typically, functionalization is a wafer-level process, of which screen and inkjet printing, dispensing and direct atomic layer processing are good examples. Once the sensor wafer is fully processed and functionalized, it must be singulated onto individual sensor dies. After that the individual sensor die will be assembled. Various die singulation methods have been reported, but they can pose serious problems for the functionalized sensor wafer. The sensing materials used for functionalization are dominated by metal-oxides, which are sensitive to environmental factors, including thermal exposure, humidity uptake, etc. In this paper, we reviewed various die singulation techniques and methods, in function of their suitability for singulating fully functionalized metal-oxide (MOX) micro-hotplates sensor silicon wafers, including wafer sawing, laser ablation and dicing, scribe-and-break, stealth dicing, plasma dicing, dicing before grinding and others. Finally, we identified the most suitable wafer singulation method for the selected application and presented an outlook.

articleTitle: Innovative Active Cell Balancing Circuit Using Common Capacitor for Energy Redistribution
abstract: This paper introduces the working principle and design of an innovative active cell balancing circuit using a common capacitor for energy redistribution. The common capacitor is, in fact, a supercapacitor (SCAP), able to fulfil the time requirements for discharging or charging a battery cell. The energy transfer is accomplished in two stages: charge is moved from the most charged cell to the SCAP, and from the SCAP to the least charged cell. Between each cell and the SCAP there are two integrated-circuit (IC) isolated DC/DC converters, a step-up and a step-down one, their role being to guarantee a negligible energy loss during transfer, a high control over the charging and discharging currents without the need of additional components and a simple and straightforward way to connect each cell to its corresponding converter. Two switches separate the converter ICs from any power source when they are not used. The microcontroller operates the switches, creating the path for the energy transfer. This proposed four-cell balancing topology proves to be solving the main issues of the already existing active cell balancing methods: it involves a small, simple circuit, an uncomplicated control algorithm, a reduced number of electronic components, a low energy loss, an easy and straightforward selection of the most and least charged cells, no need for thermal management, equalization times dependent only on the choice of the DC-DC converter ICs and high control over charging and discharging currents.

articleTitle: Thermal-Mechanical Analysis of Electroplated Copper for IC Packaging
abstract: This paper examines the temperature-dependent mechanical properties of an electroplated copper film. The stress in a 3μm thick copper film electroplated on a 775μm thick silicon substrate was measured using a custom-built setup based on a laser optical method. The thermal cycling covered a temperature range from room temperature to 420°C, revealing that the films exhibit stress relaxation at elevated temperatures and significant strain hardening during thermal cycling. Continuum plasticity analyses indicate that the experimentally measured stress-temperature response can only be represented with a combined isotropic-kinematic hardening model. The parameters of the model were identified by minimizing the difference between the experimental results and a Finite Element model, which successfully predicts the stress-temperature hysteresis observed during thermal cycling. The research also delves into the effects of thermal cycling on the mechanical characteristics of electroplated copper. The reduction in hardness observed post-thermal cycling which may suggest grain growth as reported in literature. Despite this Young's modulus value of the copper film under investigation remained unchanged after thermal cycling.

articleTitle: Full-Field IR-Thermography for Bond-Quality Inspection of Electroplated Aluminium Interconnects for Cryo-SiP Architectures
abstract: This paper addresses thermal transient IR thermography as full-field and non-destructive failure analytical technique to determine the bond quality of microelectronic joints, exploiting the transparency of a silicon chip for MIR photons. The method is exemplified for C2C bonded electroplated Aluminium joints as they could come in as a novel joining technology for 3D heterogeneously integrated Cryo-SiP architectures for ion-trap based quantum computers. We have evaluated the method experimentally for different thermosonic bond parameters and validated it by metallographic sectioning. First results are shown. We could derive that the phase and amplitude image could be used to detect defects in the joints with good sensitivity and within reasonable testing times. This method could have potential to determine zero-hour quality of such joints during inline testing.

articleTitle: Massive Parallel Assembly and Interconnection for Micro-LEDs – a Technical Feasibility Study
abstract: This paper does not only present the RGB handling but also the electrical bonding of Micro-LED arranged onto a display. Micro-LEDs are getting more and more attractive for micro-screen applications since allowing energy saving for mobile applications. The present paper showcases a soldering based assembly technology to bond several thousand small size LED chips to a larger area substrate. The assembly of “RGB” micro-chips on a host substrate are presented using the developed assembly technology suitable for display applications using three individual “LED wafers”. The process combines handling of small size chips (ca. 20×20 µm) by a conveyor from a donor wafer (a flipped source wafer) to the soldering onto target substrate for reliable electrical connection. The component soldering is performed by a three steps sequential assembly to achieve the placement and final bonding inclusive electrical interconnects by AuSn soldering of three different chips of same size arranged in a 150×150 matrix array. A yield of 99.5 % of correctly connected die could be achieved within this demonstrative study of massive parallel assembly.

articleTitle: Study of the Water and Steam Resistance of Thick Film Materials for Sensor Application Up to 300°C
abstract: The present study focuses on the durability of regular thick film materials for sensor applications in harsh water/steam environment by autoclave storage. Two experiments have been carried out. The first experimental run focuses on insulating materials typically used for thick film manufacturing. Two glass based overglazes, a glass based dielectric paste as well as the polymers PEEK and polyimide were tested in five consecutive autoclave experiments ranging from 110 °C/0.16 MPa to 287 °C/7.03 MPa, with a storage time of approx. 48 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$h$</tex> per run. Weight measurements and optical investigations after each experiment showed, that all glass-based insulators failed already during the 172 °C/0.83 MPa storage. The polyimide failed at 222 °C/2.37 MPa and the PEEK layer survived but started to lose adhesion to the substrate during the 172°C storage. It has been shown that the standard 96 % Al<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>thick film substrate is not suitable for this environment and shows strong degradation, while high purity 99.6 % Al<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>and ZrO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>(Y<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>stabilized) resist even 290 °C/7.35 MPa. A second set of experiments focuses on the application of mostly metallic passivation layers for these vulnerable insulators. The results show that double layers of the investigated AgPt and Au thick film pastes are most reliable even at 290 °C/7.35 MPa, while single layers of AgPt and Pt paste offer no hermetic sealing and cause failure. Thin Ti films (300 nm and 500 nm) show good passivation capabilities at 152 °C/0.5 MPa but fail at 290 °C/7.35 MPa. The results indicate the difficulties of applying standard thick film technologies for sensor applications in a water/steam environment above 150°C and imply the necessity of new technology and material developments for such applications.

articleTitle: Parylene as a Novel Packaging Material for Adhesive Bonding, Flexible Electronics and Wafer Level Packaging
abstract: Advanced packaging technologies are the main driver for the growth of the packaging market. However, to enable them, new materials with improved properties are crucial. Parylene refers to the thermoplastic polymer family of Poly(para-xylylene), which unites an outstanding combination of excellent properties. This study aims to present an overview about recent research with respect to the usage of Parylene for packaging and integration. This includes the usage of Parylene for adhesive wafer and chip bonding, the realization of ultra-thin flexible circuit boards as well as for wafer level packaging. For bonding, Parylene can be used as an adhesive. Doing so, the different Parylene types address different temperature ranges between <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$280^{\circ}\mathrm{C}/300^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$</tex> (Parylene C) and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$420^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$</tex> (Parylene N) / <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$430^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$</tex> (Parylene F) and provide excellent bonding strengths, i.e. <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(38.0\pm 7.6)$</tex> MPa tensile strength and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(85.5\pm 11.0)$</tex> MPa shear strength. Furthermore, a new technology for the realization of ultra-thin printed circuit boards (PCB) based on Parylene was developed. These PCBs use Parylene as a substrate, a dielectric as well as an encapsulation layer and feature multiple metallic redistribution layers at a total thickness of only 20 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu \mathrm{m}$</tex> or even less. Advanced and wafer level packaging based on Parylene can be achieved by combining the results for Parylene adhesive bonding the ultra-thin flexible Parylene PCB. Doing so, different approaches are discussed.

articleTitle: Investigating the Failure Mechanisms of Electromigration and Copper Oxide Formation in Fine-Pitch Cu RDL
abstract: Fine pitch copper traces raise electromigration concerns due to high current density. This study investigates the failure mechanism in passivated copper lines. Three passivation types were tested: polymer, silicon nitride <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\text{Si}_{3}\mathrm{N}_{4})$</tex>, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\text{Si}_{3}\mathrm{N}_{4}$</tex> 'silicon dioxide <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\text{SiO}_{2})$</tex> bilayer. Separate storage tests confirmed that temperature alone (no current) in a normal oven can degrade polymer-coated copper lines, likely due to oxygen diffusion through polymer and copper oxide formation. Electromigration testing on the polymer type showed similar damage as the normal oven storage test, suggesting oxide formation dominated failure. In contrast, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\text{Si}_{3}\mathrm{N}_{4}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\text{Si}_{3}\mathrm{N}_{4}/\text{SiO}_{2}$</tex> prevented copper oxide formation, highlighting their potential for improved reliability.

articleTitle: The Potential of Machine Learning for Thermal Modelling of SiC Power Modules - A Review
abstract: The introduction of silicon carbide(SiC) has reduced the superiority of traditional silicon-based power module pack-aging strategies. As packaging strategies become increasingly complex, classical thermal modelling tools often prove inadequate in balancing efficiency with accuracy. Integrating these tools with machine learning (ML) can significantly enhance their application potential. This discussion commences by addressing the pressing issues in thermal modelling of SiC modules, specifically the challenges associated with multiple heat sources and heat spreading. During the design stage, ML models can swiftly simulate the thermal response of various packaging strategies, aiding engineers in eliminating ineffective options. In the monitoring phase, the employment of a digital twin enables a deeper investigation into degradation phenomena. This article reviews the current status and explores the potential applications of ML in thermal modelling of SiC power modules.

articleTitle: Reliability Analysis of Surface Mount Interconnect Technologies Suitable for Temperatures Up to 200°C
abstract: In recent years there has been an increased need for high-temperature-resistant electronics both in power electronics and in robust sensor systems for industrial applications. This is often linked to the development of new materials and technologies. However, there are a number of applications where the use of SMT or THT-compatible components and interconnect technologies is an alternative for both cost reasons and the load scenario. This paper presents reliability studies for the manufacturing of high-temperature-resistant electronics in SMT assembly based on commercial components for the isothermal load case of 200°C. The evaluation criteria include both the electrical properties and the consideration of the shear strengths with the associated fracture patterns.

articleTitle: AI-Driven Digital Twin for Health Monitoring of Wide Band Gap Power Semiconductors
abstract: A significant challenge in the implementation of health monitoring systems for estimating the health state of devices is the lack of accurate information about design details. This challenge is particularly prominent in the field of power electronics, where both IC designers and converter designers are often hesitant to share information about their designs. Addressing this issue, this paper introduces a novel AI-driven digital twin modeling methodology that enables the detection and classification of failures in power semiconductors, particularly Wide Band Gap semiconductors. By employing AI-based system identification techniques, this method offers a noninvasive approach to health monitoring of power switches with high resolution, even while operating under real conditions. The proposed method has been validated by simulating wire bond failure in a SiC power MOSFET using MATLAB SIMULINK, and the results demonstrate its accuracy.

articleTitle: Low Temperature Die-Attach Bonding Using Copper Particle Free Inks
abstract: The paper presents the potential of a particle-free copper ink, based on a complexed metal salt, with regard to increasing performance requirements, particularly in terms of thermal conductivity and lower bondline thicknesses. The copper ink is applied on ENEPIG and copper substrates. An integral aspect of the research is the designed predrying process, in which nanoparticles are generated in Situ using formic acid-enriched nitrogen. As optimal conditions a predrying for 10 min at 130°C was investigated, to have still sufficient tack for the chip placing and already during predrying generated nanoparticles. The formation of Cu nanoparticles caused by the thermal decomposition of the metal salt, both during predrying and sintering, is another important aspect. The predrying process is critical to achieve a homogeneous surface thickness on which the chip is sintered. In the following process, the chips are sintered under nitrogen under a pressure of 15 or 30 MPa for 5 or 15 min at 250°C. The results show the successful realization of a homogeneous, thin copper sintered layer (6 μm) by sintering for 15 min at 30 MPa and 250°C under nitrogen. For this process conditions an average shear strength of 53 ± 9 MPa for a copper-copper bond was achieved. With slightly different sintering conditions of 225 °C, 15 minutes and 30 MPa, shear forces of 42 ±3 MPa were achieved. The tests with ENEPIG boards and chips also show comparable shear values, with 42 ± 2 MPa under optimum sintering conditions. The fracture from shearing was detected within the interconnect. With further increasing the homogeneous layer thickness, the applied sinter pressure can be reduced.

articleTitle: Solid-State Growth Kinetics of Compound Layers in Electroplated Cu-In Layer Systems
abstract: Low-temperature bonding technologies for advanced packaging are of substantial interest since they may enable the integration of a wide variety of components into highly integrated electronic systems. Replacing Sn in fine-pitch interconnects with In presents a viable approach for reducing the required bonding temperature while still exploiting the distinct benefits of liquid interlayers for joint formation. The technological feasibility of Cu-In microbumps depends at first on the grade and scale of interfacial metallurgical reactions. The present study is the first one addressing the growth kinetics of Cu-In compounds in electroplated Cu-In thin films. The results show a homogeneous growth of CuIn<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> up to 80 °C with a layer thickening proportional to the cubic root of the reaction time. The growth behavior is thus mainly controlled by grain-boundary diffusion and associated with an activation energy of 44 kJ/mol. The derived growth model is valid for compound layer thicknesses up to approx. 4 µm, above which volume-diffusion controlled growth becomes the primary mechanism. For temperatures above 100 °C, Cu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">11</inf>In<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">9</inf> predominantly grows in an inhomogeneous way, but the average layer thickening obeys a t<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1/3</sup>-law. The growth rates are heavily impacted by the temperature, which is reflected by an activation energy of 76 kJ/mol. The cross-sections of the prepared samples and the derived growth models give novel insights into the early-stage growth behavior and kinetics, respectively, of Cu-In-based compound layers. The derived data provide an essential basis for developing criteria of technological parameters for the formation of Cu-In based fine-pitch joints.

articleTitle: Improving the Thermal Management of Power LED Arrays with Diamond
abstract: The continuous increase of power density levels in components such as RF HEMTs or power LEDs and SiPs often leads to elevated hotspot temperatures that bring along reliability issues. Extracting and transferring the heat from the hotspot to the package and heatsink is however becoming increasingly difficult. One possible solution is the integration of materials with high thermal conductivity at package or board levels. Artificial diamond manufactured by chemical vapor deposition can have a thermal conductivity as high as 1800 W/m-K., a value 4.5 times higher than Cu. In this work we evaluate the potential of mounting several LEDs on diamond boards. To this end, the thermal profile of a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2\times 2$</tex> array of Cree XLamp XB-D LEDs mounted on MCPCBs and diamond boards was evaluated using Ansys. The impact of replacing the AIN die-carrier in the LED package with diamond was also evaluated. Due to the low thermal conductivity of the MCPCB dielectric layer, replacing the board with diamond has a larger impact than replacing the AIN die-carrier. The thermal benefit of diamond increases as thermal power density rises, either by increasing current levels or by bringing the LEDs closer to one another - even though replacing the MCPCB with a diamond board may induce thermal cross-talk between individual LEDs. By replacing both die-carrier and MCPCB with diamond, for 700 mA the aging of the LEDs slows down <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\approx$</tex> 79-97% depending on the activation energy of the failure mechanisms. Further benefit can be obtained by using die-attach, solders and thermal interface materials and solders with high thermal conductivity.

articleTitle: Analysis of LED Solder Joints During Combined Power and Thermal Cycling
abstract: VLS's lighting products offer enhanced brightness along with intelligent features and sustainable solutions to decrease CO2 emissions. These new features ensure an optimal driving experience, prioritizing safety and comfort for both drivers and pedestrians. The reliability of the electronic systems is confirmed through standard tests like power cycling or thermal cycling. VLS is also working on simulation solutions to numerically validate the design and reliability of these electronic systems. A cause of failure in thermal shock tests is the thermal fatigue of solder joints, resulting from repeated thermal stresses on the assembly caused by the mismatch in Coefficient of Thermal Expansion (CTE) between the LED and the substrate. The primary focus has been on developing a predictive simulation method to assess the reliability of LED assemblies under combined power and thermal cycling. In this study, we delineate the steps involved in validating the simulation of combined power and thermal cycles in LED systems. Using thermomechanical simulations, we examine the cumulative damage to solder joints caused by both thermal cycling and power cycling. In a combined power thermal cycling test, the electronic system experiences a combination of high cycle fatigue (HCL) due to power cycling (several million cycles) and low fatigue damage (LCF) from thermal cycles. In order to consider the combined fatigue damages due to those two loadings a new approach was considered. Firstly, we will begin by analyzing the spatial and temporal evolution of temperature within the assembly through transient thermal simulations. Subsequently, based on these temperature variations, we conduct a decomposition of damage analysis between HCF and LFC models, examining them independently. The Low cycle fatigue model was validated by comparing the fatigue life prediction with results from thermal cycle testing. Following this, we assessed the cumulative damage of HCL and LCF by comparing it with outcomes from combined power thermal cycle testing. Finally, we establish a correlation between the experimental number of cycles at failure and the cracked surface observed with dye penetrant to evaluate the accuracy of our model's assumptions. This new method demonstrates promising predictive capability for combined power thermal cycle testing results, while also enhancing our understanding of design parameters that accelerate failures.

articleTitle: Prediction of High Strain Rate Properties of Bi-Doped SnAgCu Solders after Sustained High-Temperature Operation
abstract: Electronics in automotive and aerospace applications may need sustained high-temperature exposure ranging from 150 to 200°C, as well as variable mechanical stress and vibration. Additionally, electronics may be housed in non-climate-controlled containers for lengthy periods of time prior to deployment. The industry has experimented with adding dopants to SAC solders to mitigate the harmful consequences of prolonged high-temperature exposure. There is minimal information available on the mechanical performance, reliability, and constitutive models of novel formulations. The purpose of this work is to fill a gap in existing research by assessing the influence of Bismuth addition on the characteristics of SAC-Bi alloys at low temperatures, high strain rates, and varied thermal aging durations of up to a year. Several doped alloys, including SAC-Q, SAC-R, M758, QSAC10, QSAC20, and SAC305 solder, have been examined in a strain-rate range of 1–100 per second in the temperature range of -65°C to +200°C after one year of prolonged exposure to 50°C and 100°C. Based on the trends of mechanical properties with respect to Bismuth content in solders, UTS and E are predicted for the solder alloy SAC+4%Bi. The Anand parameters were calculated and used to assess the correctness of the Anand model by comparing experimentally observed data to anticipated data using the computed model constants. In order to ascertain the hysteresis loops and plastic work densities, the Anand parameters have been included in an FE framework to simulate drop occurrences for a ball-grid array packed on a printed circuit board assembly. It has been demonstrated that under continuous high-temperature operation, an increase in the bismuth concentration reduces the UTS deterioration and elastic modulus at high strain rates.

articleTitle: Reduced-Order Modelling for Coupled Thermal-Mechanical Analysis and Reliability Assessment of Power Electronic Modules with Nonlinear Material Behaviours
abstract: This paper presents a compact and time-efficient reduced-order modelling method for thermal-mechanical analysis and material nonlinearity study of power electronics modules (PEMs). Generally, the thermal-mechanical analyses in research are conducted utilising a sequential coupling method, where the thermal model is solved first, and the temperature distributions are used as a load in the structural (mechanical) system. The direct-coupling method has been employed in the present thermomechanical analysis to evaluate the thermal and structural governing equations together, i.e., to solve for its thermal and directional deformation distributions, which are degrees of freedom (DOFs) of the coupled system. A new approach, utilising the Krylov-subspace- and Arnoldi-based model order reduction (MOR) technique, Newmark method and Newton-Raphson al-gorithm within the reduced-order modelling framework, has been developed and demonstrated here for analysing material nonlinearity of PEMs. The reduced-order model (ROM) solutions agree exceptionally well with the full-order (FOM) solutions, showing excellent consistency in inelastic strains and plastic work results for materials with time-independent and time-dependent nonlinearities. The MOR method offers a remarkably compact model with a ROM order of just 20x20 for reduced-order computation compared to a FOM order of about 400,000x400,000 and up to 83% reduction in computational time.

articleTitle: Advancements in Epoxy Pattern Quality Checks: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence for Enhanced Low-Contrast Contour Analysis
abstract: To have ideal wetting, bond line thickness, and flanks surrounding a die after bonding the dispense quality is crucial. Depending on the used epoxy material, dispensed volume, and substrate the contrast to properly detect the dispensed pattern can be challenging. There are different approaches to mitigate this issue with obvious ones like different angles of illumination, wavelength, polarization, or improved vision algorithm. However, using conventional contrast based or gradient dependent detection routines are depending on contrast value, which can fail and do not generalize the solution to quality assessment. In this article we first go through the low contrast solution used in our conventional pipeline to improve the results and then present an artificial intelligence (AI) approach to overcome the limitations of current epoxy pattern inspection methodologies in a die bonder at production throughput. Evaluated on 3 verification datasets the detection precision for both methods shows promising results being higher than 90 percent.

articleTitle: Electromigration Reliability of Cu3Sn Microbumps for 3D Heterogeneous Integration
abstract: 3D heterogeneous integration (HI) and advanced packaging (AP) technologies require small volume, high-density interconnects for stacking discrete chips for which the reliability of interconnects becomes crucial. Intermetallic compounds (IMCs) based μbumps have been shown to outperform solder-based μbumps concerning their resistance to electromigration (EM) related failures, which is a key index to assess the interconnect reliability. Cu-Sn solid-liquid interdiffusion (SLID) bonding is an attractive low-cost wafer-level bonding technology for rapid manufacturing of full Cu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>Sn IMC μbumps, However, SLID requires melting of Sn during the bonding process which poses risks and design challenges in manufacturing. Due to Sn squeeze-out during the bonding process, Sn melt could react with redistribution layers (RDLs) or metallization layers and form IMCs at undesired locations resulting in early failures thereby compromising the reliability. The Sn-squeeze out issue during bonding is addressed in this work by designing test structures with equal and unequal lateral dimensions of μbumps in the top and bottom wafers. The effects of Sn-squeeze out on the EM resistance and reliability are compared in both designs. Significant improvement in the Sn-squeeze out and corresponding EM resistance was observed in the test structures manufactured with unequal lateral dimensions of μbumps in the top and bottom wafers. FE element simulations were carried out to gain insights and assess the impact of Sn squeeze-out on the reliability and functionality of the Cu<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>Sn μbumps.

articleTitle: Effect of Electromigration on Micro Tensile Test Mechanical Properties and Micro Structure of Pure Copper
abstract: Copper as the fine pitch circuit line material of advanced electronic packaging substrate will experience tensile stress during manufacturing as well as electronic application. Electromigration will induce electromigration force and Joule heat to the circuit line during electronic application. It is imaginable that electromigration will have impact on the mechanical properties and microstructure of the copper circuit. In this study, we investigated the effect of electromigration on the micro tensile mechanical property of pure copper, and the mechanism was explored by incorporating the microstructure evolutions. The pure copper specimens were pre-annealed at 678°C for 12 hours to reduce the residual stress generated during fabrication. The subsequent current stressing treatments at different current densities (2~ 3× 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</sup> A/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>) were found to enhance the yield strength up to 89%, Young's modulus 96.2%, and ultimate tensile strength 6.5%, whereas degrade elongation by 5.5%. The electron backscatter diffraction analysis showed that non-deformation recrystallization occurred which induced grain refining and twin formation of Cu. The influence of dislocation, twin fraction, and grain orientation on the mechanical properties were investigated and discussed in the study. The athermal electron wind force effect was found predominated over the thermal Joule heat on governing the microstructure variation and the mechanical properties.

articleTitle: Innovative System-in-Package Building Blocks for Future Space Applications
abstract: This paper deals with the development of System in Package building blocks for both power and digital space application. The first building block focuses on embedding technology for Power converter featuring high current and very low voltage. A conversion cell building block using transistors GaN as fast switching element and their control electronics was developed using solder embedded technology with R-1566S Flame Retardant (FR4) material. The second building block concerns build-up substrate for advanced digital System-in-Package (SiP). Considering the high pin count dies with fine pitch to fan out, the build-up substrate resulted in a core substrate surrounded by 6 build-up materials on both sides namely a 6-N-6 structure. Resin Coated Copper (RCC) R-G740M resin presenting ultra low modulus and very low Dielectric constant (Dk) was selected as build-up material. For both building blocks, the materials physico-chemical characteristics were analyzed. Then test vehicle architectures were defined taking into account space application specificities as well as design for manufacturing (dfm) rules. Finally, test vehicles were manufactured and initial characterizations were made including visual inspection, X-Ray technique, and cross-section. Finally, the testing approach for reliability evaluation in space condition was defined based on existing International Process Circuit (IPC) and European Cooperation for Space Standardization (ECSS) standards for conventional Printed Circuit Board (PCB) and assembly qualification.

articleTitle: Fully Connected Neural Network (FCNN) Based Validation Framework for FEA Post Processing to Improve SAC Solder Reliability Analysis
abstract: The reliability of solder joints in high-power LED packages is crucial for the automotive industry. Finite Element Analysis (FEA) is the widespread approach for predicting the crack growth in solder interconnects. Focusing on the thermo-mechanical stresses between LED package and the PCB, i.e. the aluminum insulated metal substrate (Al-IMS), this paper discusses the reliability of different LED package designs and solder materials, using enhanced FEA post-processing and Fully Connected Neural Network (FCNN) based lifetime model. The analysis includes seven different ceramic-based LED packages with four solders, evaluating crack formation in the solder joints across common two-pad and three-pad footprint designs, using data from an extensive experimental reliability study. The study not only compares the behavior of commonly used SAC305 and SAC105 solders using state-of-the-art parameters from literature but also extract the Garofalo creep model parameters for solders like Innolot <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\text{SAC}387+\text{SbInNi})$</tex> and Senju M40 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\text{SAC}107+\text{BiIn})$</tex> using experimental strain rate measurements at various temperatures. The research further discusses about the different FEA post-processing techniques suited for Surface Mounted Devices (SMD) LED assemblies, highlighting the limitations of methods traditionally used for Ball Grid Array (BGA) packages due to significant differences in geometry and pad layout. The primary objective of the FEA model is to accurately predict the reliability of various pad designs-whether two-pad or three-pad footprints and to develop a lifetime model. Furthermore, instead of using Coffin Manson equation FCNN are employed for the lifetime prediction of the solder joints with multiple inputs to capture the nonlinear relationship between the data. The results indicate that the model shows good agreement for ceramic LED packages, achieving an <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{R}^{2}$</tex> score of 0.87 for critical path averaging. However, some variability is noted for ceramic LED packages with thin film copper metallization on the ceramic, which exhibit different behavior compared to packages with thick film metallization. Also, SAC305 and SAC105 showed improved accuracy with actual values when using FCNN compared to Coffin Manson equation used previously [6], while <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\text{SAC}387+\text{SbBiNi}$</tex> exhibited the largest errors followed by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\text{SAC}107+\text{BiIn}$</tex>, likely due to uncertainties in extracting the creep parameter for the Garafalo model from the experimental data. This suggests the need for more detailed experimentation and refinement of the Garofalo model parameters for better accuracy.

articleTitle: Passive Intermodulation Estimation of a Novel Printed Circuit Board Interconnection Technology Based on Static I-V
abstract: This paper presents a novel printed circuit board (PCB) interconnection technology known as KlettWelding, proposed as a potential solution to reduce passive intermodulation (PIM) in mobile communication devices. This room-temperature technology is used for stacking PCBs similar to spring contacts, which are widely employed in mobile devices to establish electrical connections. A concept is introduced to make stacked PCBs interconnections feasible based on different stacked pads interconnection (SPI) geometries. A third-order PIM estimation method based on current-voltage (I-V) behavior is used to estimate third-order PIM products of the achieved SPIs. Numerical calculations demonstrate that the SPIs have third-order PIM products in the range of -212.4 dBm to -324.9 dBm for an input power range of 10 dBm to 20 dBm. Recommendations for possible future analyses are discussed.

articleTitle: Alignment Between Subsequent 3D Molding Layers for Optimized Performance of 3D Integrated Patch Antennas for Advanced Sensing Applications
abstract: In the context of Fan-Out Wafer Level Packaging (FOWLP) has gained significant momentum in the market in recent years, as it meets the substantial demand for miniaturization and offers exceptional scalability, as well as electrical and thermal performance. Herein, compression molding is a standard process to encapsulate microelectronic components, which serves the purpose of protecting components from mechanical stress, as well as moisture and contamination. Furthermore, it provides the necessary area to fan out electrical contacts to route signals within the package. Commonly used materials are highly filled epoxy resins (epoxy molding compound, EMC). Recent research has been focused on the exploration of 3D-compression molding, with the objective to deploy nonplanar shapes to enable the potential of 3D freeform antennas, which allow for a significant increase in the field of view (FOV) [1]. For this, multi-step 3D molding is required, as ground and signal metallization layers, formed utilizing direct Cu metallization, are separated by EMC. Accurate alignment between subsequent molding layers and hence corresponding Cu layers (ground and signal) is required for proper performance. In compression molding, such alignment steps are typically not required. We investigate various alignment concepts to achieve accurate alignment in lateral (x-y) direction. By thorough evaluation of achieved tolerances for the respective concepts, we propose preferred options for advancing multilayer 3D molding approaches. This will ultimately enhance the performance of 3D integrated antennas and enable the extension of this approach to applications beyond package integrated antennas.

articleTitle: Automatized Multi-objective Optimization for Reliability of Power Electronics
abstract: In all automotive electrical vehicle solutions (EV, HEV, FCEV, etc.) power electronics technologies process power for charging, drive train or supply for other electric units. The main goal in the development of power electronics is to fulfill required reliability at lowest cost. Active functional loads cause temperature changes and primarily contribute to reliability of power electronics. All focus components - such as power stage, DC-link, and EMC filter elements - need to be analyzed through advanced DfR (Design-for-Reliability) methods in the most efficient way. Thus, a method and framework for fast and automatized virtual design of experiments (vDoE) are required to optimize reliability of power electronics from early development stage based on a high number of design variants and load cycles. The established framework includes automatically connected simulations from power loss, through thermal and thermo-mechanics to failure probability and lifetime assessments.

articleTitle: Reliability Testing and Virtual Prototyping for Embedded GaN Power Modules in Automotive Applications
abstract: The electrification of road transport requires new inverter solutions. GaN power devices offer substantial advantages in terms of electrical performance compared to Si devices and in terms of cost compared to their SiC counterparts. Embedding the semiconductor devices into organic laminates leads to very effective production technologies and robust structures with a small form factor that can be assembled with the drivetrain easily. This study focuses on the reliability of such embedded GaN power modules. During testing and operation, the module is exposed to thermal swings caused by the environment and the substantial power dissipation in the GaN device. They impose cyclic mechanical stresses within the semiconductor chips, the metallic interconnects, the organic laminates and at all interfaces between them due to the large differences in thermal expansion and stiffness of the different materials. At some critical points, the stresses can exceed the elastic range. Inelastic cyclic loading is known to cause fatigue, cracking, and failure. Therefore, reliability testing is an essential part of module development. It involves passive and active temperature cycling. The passive tests simulate the ambient conditions, e.g., the heating and cooling of the motor to which the inverter is attached, while the active power cycle test represents the operation of the module. Although the tests reasonably exaggerate the load conditions so that degradation is accelerated, they still take several weeks or even months. Virtual tests based on numerical simulations can reduce this time to a few hours. However, the virtual models and simulation results must first be calibrated and validated before they can credibly replace the physical tests. The paper covers the reliability tests, whose conditions need some adjustment to accommodate GaN devices, and presents a strategy to develop models capable of providing credible simulation results. Using the calibrated models, the measured material data has been involved to study the effect of different copper qualities on the stress level and the risk of failure. Based on this, recommendations are deduced for optimizing the module design to improve its reliability. The testing part describes the setup and presents the essential results of the passive and active thermal cycling in the form of measured data and results from the physical failure analysis. In addition, the results of dedicated material characterization are included. The simulation part describes the model creation based on a modular concept and presents the simulation results obtained in parallel to the physical passive and active temperature cycle tests based on material data from open literature. Once the tests were completed, the simulation results have been compared to the experimental findings. They agreed qualitatively but showed differences in the quantities. Adjusting the thermal boundary conditions as well as some geometric details, the simulation was repeated until the quantitative differences diminished

articleTitle: Authors' Index of All Technical Papers Presented at the Conference; "Electronics System-Integration Technology Conference" ESTC 2024
Proceedings for Publication in IEEE Xplore
